Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Disagreement over verses like this was not limited to the question of free choice and predestination. It also produced a disagreement over God’s knowledge.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Even the Jabriyya took the same position as the Muʿtazilites on this question, despite the deep difference between them over freedom and predestination.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Jahm, whom we have already seen was a leading figure of the Jabriyya, raised the question of “God’s knowledge” before the Muʿtazilites did.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He argued that God’s knowledge is not eternal, despite the apparent meaning of the verses just quoted. Instead, this knowledge comes into being.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Here again, Jahm goes back to the position he had already taken on the divine attributes. Knowledge is an attribute. Since he had denied attributes to God, what could he now say about God’s knowledge?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Could he simply deny that God knows?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He could not accept that conclusion, because denying God knowledge would mean attributing ignorance to Him. Jahm was not prepared to say that.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
So how did he solve the problem?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Once again, he used a rational method that comes close to philosophical reasoning.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Ibn Ḥazm reports Jahm as setting out the problem in these terms:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“If God’s knowledge had always existed, then it must either be God Himself or something other than Him. If God’s knowledge is something other than God and has also existed eternally, then this means associating something with God”—that is, making knowledge a partner alongside God, since there would now be two eternal realities: God and His knowledge—“and giving eternity to something other than God. This is unbelief. But if God’s knowledge is God Himself, then God is knowledge”—meaning that “God” would simply mean “knowledge”—“and this is heresy.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
What Jahm means in the last part is that if God Himself is simply identical with knowledge, then what truly exists is knowledge, rather than God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Jahm has now stated the problem in philosophical terms. But how does he solve it?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

He chooses a solution that denies the eternity of God’s knowledge without denying knowledge to God altogether. In other words, he says that God’s knowledge arises in time rather than existing eternally.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But this immediately raises more questions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

How does this knowledge arise? How does God come to know something that He did not know before? Does He know a thing before it exists, or only when it comes into existence? And when this new knowledge arises, where does it exist? In what “locus,” or subject, does this newly arising knowledge of God exist?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Historians of the Islamic schools give somewhat different answers to these questions, apart from the last one.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The reason is that no book written by Jahm himself has survived, so we cannot read his views directly. In later centuries, his ideas and the basic principles of his doctrine became known through works describing the different Islamic schools and sects, as well as through historical and literary works from that period.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

A number of major historians of Arab-Islamic thought discussed this particular question in their accounts of Jahm, including al-Shahrastānī, al-Ashʿarī, al-Baghdādī, al-Ṣafadī, Ibn Taymiyya, and others.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Al-Shahrastānī answers the questions above by saying that Jahm accepted newly arising instances of knowledge for God that existed in no particular locus.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He then reports Jahm as saying:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“It is not possible for God to know a thing before creating it. For if He knew it and then created it, would His knowledge remain as it was, or would it not? If it remained as it was, it would become ignorance, because knowing that a thing will exist is different from knowing that it has already come into existence. But if His knowledge did not remain as it was, then it changed. And whatever changes is created, not eternal.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
After quoting this, al-Shahrastānī says that Jahm’s position agrees here with that of Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He then gives the rest of Jahm’s argument:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“Once it is established that knowledge comes into being, there are only two possibilities. Either God’s knowledge comes into being within His own essence, which would mean that His essence changes and that God becomes a place in which new events occur. Or it comes into being in some other locus, in which case that locus would be the thing described as possessing the knowledge, not the Creator Himself. It therefore follows that this knowledge exists in no locus.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Al-Shahrastānī then says that Jahm accepted “newly arising instances of knowledge as numerous as the things known.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This account gives us a fairly complete picture of how Jahm tried to solve the problem.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

God’s knowledge, on this view, is not eternal but arises in time. This divine knowledge exists in no locus. Nor is it one single, universal knowledge that contains everything. Instead, God has knowledge of individual things, and these instances of knowledge multiply according to the number of individual things that exist and become known to Him.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The question of whether God knows particulars rather than universals would later become one of the major points of disagreement between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites. Here again, Jahm anticipated a later problem in kalām.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
From al-Shahrastānī’s account, we can understand Jahm to mean that God cannot know a thing before that thing exists.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But al-Ashʿarī reports two different views from Jahm on this part of the question.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
According to the first, Jahm allowed that God might know all things before they exist through a kind of knowledge that God brings into being before them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But al-Ashʿarī then reports another account that says the opposite:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“Someone else reported the opposite from him, claiming that God knows a thing at the moment it comes into existence. It is impossible for a thing to be known while it does not exist”—that is, before it comes into being—“because for Jahm, a ‘thing’ is an existing body. What does not exist is not a thing, and therefore cannot be known or unknown.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

When we compare this second account with what al-Shahrastānī reports, and with the similar accounts found in al-Baghdādī and al-Ṣafadī, there is good reason to think that Jahm believed God’s knowledge of a thing arises when the thing itself comes into existence, not before.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But our main concern here is not to settle historically which of these two positions Jahm actually held.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
What matters most is the way he thought about the problem and tried to solve it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

From the statements attributed to him by the major historians of the Islamic schools, we can see that this determinist thinker relied on a rational method very close to philosophical reasoning. Even when dealing with these metaphysical questions, he worked with abstract concepts.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There is, however, a contradiction in Jahm’s thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
It appears in the tension between his determinism and his strong insistence on denying knowledge as an eternal attribute of God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

If God has no prior knowledge of human actions that will happen later, then those actions are not known to Him in advance. They therefore cannot be governed in advance by divine will. At that point, determinism falls away and human choice returns.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Here we find another development beyond the way the Khārijites had treated this question earlier.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
For most Muslims, the usual understanding of faith had two parts: first, belief in God and His messengers; and second, openly declaring that belief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The Khārijites then added a third element: acting according to that belief. In their view, there could be no true faith unless belief and profession were joined by action.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
With Jahm, however, the meaning of faith takes on a new form.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He reduces it to a single new element: knowledge.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Faith, in Jahm’s view, means knowing God, His messengers, and everything that comes from God. Nothing else counts as faith.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī describes Jahm’s doctrine in these words:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“Faith is knowledge alone. Everything apart from knowledge—professing it with the tongue, submitting and surrendering to God and His Messenger, honoring them, fearing them, and performing acts with the body—is not faith.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Al-Shahrastānī gives Jahm’s position in another form:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“If someone gains knowledge and then denies it with his tongue, that denial does not make him an unbeliever, because knowledge does not disappear through denial. He therefore remains a believer.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Al-Shahrastānī adds an important point. Speaking for Jahm, he says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
In other words, it cannot be broken down into belief, speech, and action.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He then adds another statement from Jahm:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Nor do believers differ in the degree of their faith. The faith of the prophets and the faith of the community are of one kind, because knowledge itself does not differ in degree.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Al-Baghdādī gives the same doctrine in essentially the same form.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
So what, for Jahm, is unbelief?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Unbelief is one single quality. It exists in the heart, and it is ignorance of God.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
We now have Jahm’s complete formula for faith and its opposite, unbelief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Faith is knowledge. Unbelief is ignorance.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This is genuinely a new understanding of faith. It does not simply connect faith with knowledge. It makes the two the same thing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

And if we remember that Jahm believed in knowledge reached through reason, and that he regarded reason as the first path to God even before revelation, then we can see that we are dealing with a new way of thinking.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

At this stage in the development of Arab-Islamic thought, we are beginning to reach a turning point. This new approach leads toward the rational and philosophical method later developed by the thinkers of kalām, which in turn helped prepare the way for the emergence of philosophy itself.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
One strong sign that this really was a turning point is the fierce opposition Jahm’s doctrine provoked among traditionalists.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
His rational method, whose main features we have now seen, seems to have been what most disturbed both the traditionalists and the Umayyad authorities.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

His determinism itself could fit quite comfortably with the ideology of Umayyad rule. But Jahm’s determinism was inseparable from the rational method he used to deal with the religious questions discussed above. As we have seen, he approached these questions with an unusual degree of independence and intellectual freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This bold rational tendency did not please the men who ruled the Umayyad state. On the contrary, it angered them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The class position of the Umayyad ruling order required its leaders to oppose firmly any intellectual movement that gave reason a place of its own, even a relatively independent one, outside the conservative “official” view of the state. Jahm had done precisely that.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This may have been one of the factors that led him to answer the call of al-Ḥārith ibn Surayj in Khurasan. Near the end of Umayyad rule, Ibn Surayj called on Jahm to join his war against the Umayyads. Jahm did so, and both men were killed in 128 AH.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There is another report that supports our interpretation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The Umayyad caliph Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik wrote to his representative in Khurasan, Naṣr ibn Sayyār:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“A man named Jahm has appeared in your region, one of the Dahriyya.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Here Hishām accuses Jahm of belonging to the Dahriyya.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Yet we find nothing in Jahm’s doctrine or recorded views that supports this accusation. Nor do we find even his fiercest opponents accusing him of it when they wrote against him.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Tāj al-Dīn al-Subkī, for example, attacked Jahm harshly and strongly condemned his view of faith. Yet even al-Subkī said nothing to suggest that Jahm had left Islam. In fact, he tried to interpret Jahm’s position in a way that would keep him within an Islamic framework.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Why, then, was the Umayyad ruler Hishām alone in attaching the charge of belonging to the Dahriyya to Jahm, and then using it as grounds for ordering his death?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The answer clearly cannot be Jahm’s determinism.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Determinism was itself one of the religious weapons used by the Umayyads to defend their political and class position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The more likely reason is that Jahm’s determinism existed alongside an intellectual independence from Umayyad “ideology.” It was also joined to the rational tendency that led him to give reason the leading role in dealing with some of the most sensitive religious questions of his time—questions closely tied to Islamic texts that still held the highest authority as sources of religious belief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This may be what Aḥmad Amīn meant in the statement we quoted earlier:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“Although Jahm was a determinist, he nevertheless rebelled alongside those who rose against the Umayyads. He also held views that people strongly objected to. Politics exploited the public hostility toward him and killed him.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
We should not, however, overlook another factor when trying to understand the conflict between Jahm and the Umayyad authorities that ended in his death.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Jahm was one of the mawālī. He grew up in a Persian environment in Khurasan and was attached as a client to a branch of the Arab tribe of Azd that lived there.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He also spent part of his intellectual life in Kufa.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Kufa was a place where thinkers and educated people from among the mawālī found room for political and intellectual activity against Umayyad rule. Their opposition came partly in response to the ethnic arrogance shown toward the mawālī by the Umayyad ruling order.
